I think the basic effect would be to push the prospective transhuman to the top of Maslow's Pyramid. The transhuman is likely to realize a lot of the obsessions of earlier life as stupid and irrelevant. As I often say, I hope to one day view my entire life to date as a rather awkward childhood. It is likely that with the process of being able to transfer minds will come the ability to detect and repair mental illness in very direct ways. With this technology will come a much more comprehensive understanding of the mind and the nature of personality and new definitions of normality. Much of our current social structure relates to how we've culturally tolerated certain personality disorders in certain contexts, such as how we use military training to break down our innate empathic intelligence and reluctance to kill people and how we overlook the chronic sociopathy of the wealthy despite the tremendous damage such mental illness does to the larger society when leveraged by wealth. Mind uploading may prove to be the ultimate asshole filter.

With this technology may also come a hard realization that the human being is no longer 'special' in nature. That we have no supernatural aspect that sets us apart from other kinds of life and that we must regard artificial intelligences as equals. As these old notions crumble, we may see a redefinition of old terms like 'soul' or 'spirit' to refer to the mind as a portable data construct rather than some supernatural element. Contemporary tropes always depict the artificial mind--or artilect--as broken or neurotic in some way. Devoid of emotion, literal-minded, obsessed with a quintessential human nature it can't quite match up to. The artilect is always monster, alien, or Pinocchio. But that's our own conceit. It comforts us to think that the artilect must be inherently flawed and thus inferior. That there is always some special, magical, aspect of the 'real' human that can never be duplicated. The truly scariest prospect of artificial intelligence is that might turn out just like us, which then begs the question; what are we?

I suspect that religion will adopt an attitude of denial toward the technology--as that's the compulsive response of religion to everything outside its systems. The transhuman will be declared a soulless abomination. A simulacrum of the people they once were secretly controlled by malevolent forces as a challenge to religion. The first transhuman will be declared the anti-christ. Billions of dollars will end up squandered on pseudoscientific attempts to prove the existence of the spirit. Acts of violence and terrorism may be perpetrated against this new segment of society. How might this new society respond to such attacks? What might they do to defend themselves?

We may also see a great expansion in space development resulting from this technology as we finally achieve the ultimate form of CATS. (cheap access to space) Manned spacecraft will become obsolete as we will be able to travel space by telecommunications and create settlements across the solar system that need little more than solar power for their basic life support. Perhaps the violence against transhumans and artilects will drive them off the Earth as a simple security measure.

This is true. Its important to know the difference between tired/sore/worn out muscles and when you've fucked up or stressed out your joints or ligaments.

The solution to this is to work on your form to perfection. Joint injury happens when workouts are done improperly, or with too much weight than a person can handle correctly.
Yes! I also want to mention that proper form is not only about the movement itself. It is important to focus on and isolate the muscle (or group of muscles) in order to protect the joints.

There's a couple of different things that can manifest as overdoing it. I'll try to explain some, but there are many factors that can contribute.

The first one I can think of is general weakness from poor nutrition. This can happen because of low carbohydrates over a period of time. Generally presents itself as lower lifting numbers for a session, or just lack of energy. Can be fixed by increasing carbohydrates over next couple of days.

Next one is delayed onset muscle soreness (DOMS). Usually happens to newer lifters, but can happen to changing stimulus. Usually presents as muscle soreness that lasts beyond the exercise and most likely the next day, and also lower lifting numbers. Solution is to just power through it, it will go away when your muscles have adapted. Has no effect on strength or size increases.

I'd should ask how long you have been working out, along with when the feeling of overdoing it started. It'd be curious to know about your diet as well.

Hi!

Oh no sorry, this wasn't really what I meant to ask about. I was referring to individual training sessions. For example, today I was running, and I ran at a faster pace than I usually do. I felt a little pain in my throat/neck/lower ears area and it felt like I wasn't getting enough air/oxygen. Surely this is a sign that I pushed it too hard right?

Oh, ok!

Let me first say that I'm not a doctor. Regarding the feelings you describe, that sounds normal to me when I try to run at a faster pace. The hard part is to determine if your effort during exercise warrants more rest. Determining your limit is entirely up to how you react to stress. Some people can stay at high intensity for a very long time, and some people need to keep themselves at a lower intensity. It takes time for you to determine that yourself.

Your description of symptoms reminds me of an article that I read recently.

http://www.runnersworld.com/racing/why-cant-i-run-faster

This might help. It describes the pain you feel when trying to run faster. Again, I will say that I cannot diagnose problems over the internet. If you are still concerned, I recommend going to a doctor.
This was a very informative piece, thanks a lot!

Over training? If you're feeling constantly fatigued and having trouble sleeping, you're over training. I don't know how often you work out or what type of exercise you're doing, but if you're doing strength training, you don't need to go to failure every single time, every day. If you're doing cardio or endurance, you don't need to go to the point of exhaustion every time either.

If you're in shape, you can exercise every day if you're not going to the point of exhaustion or repeatedly going to muscle failure. It's not about pushing your limits every time you work out. It's just about getting in shape and maintaining fitness once you get there.

Rest days are very important if you're just getting into shape or if you're trying to improve your fitness to another level. Your body needs recovery time or else you won't benefit from the exercise you're doing.
